papers.title: Spectral analysis of gene-dependency networks reveals emergent organization across scales in CAR T biology
papers.abstract: CAR T-cell infusion products are commonly characterized in terms of their cellular populations and transcriptional programs, but these descriptions do not fully capture how a product is organized as a system. We analyzed single-cell RNA sequencing data from the infusion products of 163 patients across eight cohorts to investigate how system-level transcriptional organization relates to both clinical outcome and how cellular features vary together across patients. For each patient, we constructed a gene-dependency graph using mutual information between the binary detection states of each gene pair across infusion cells. To characterize each patient's network architecture, we define spectral organization, O{lambda}, a measure of the relative persistence of collective patterns of gene dependence in the network. Using hierarchical Bayesian survival models, we assessed the associations of both O{lambda} and various established cellular features with treatment outcome. Higher spectral organization was associated with a higher hazard of treatment failure in both a continuous model (hazard ratio per standard deviation, 1.45, 95% credible interval 1.07-2.19) and a smooth transition model (hazard ratio comparing the high and low regimes, 2.03, 95% credible interval 1.10-3.53). When we investigated how cellular features covary across patients, we found that correlations among both T-cell programs and cell type proportions aligned more coherently with treatment failure risk in the high O{lambda} regime compared to the low regime, revealing a systems-level pattern that helps explain the clinical relevance of spectral organization. Gene set enrichment analysis further showed that more persistent architectures were associated with inflammation and cellular interaction pathways, whereas lower spectral organization was associated with biosynthetic and genome maintenance pathways, consistent with the hypothesis that the organizational state of an infusion product reflects its capacity to reconfigure in response to CAR T treatment. Altogether, our findings identify spectral organization as a property of the infusion product as a whole that connects gene-dependency architecture within individual products to the collective variation of cellular features across patients. This framework therefore motivates studying CAR T biology from a systems perspective alongside established descriptions of cellular state.

papers.title: Multimodal dynamics during naturalistic learning are associated with subsequent performance
papers.abstract: Learning from continuous material involves dynamic coordination of visual sampling, autonomic arousal, and neural activity, yet how these signals jointly organize during successful learning remains unclear. Here, we analysed synchronized eye-tracking, pupillometry, and EEG recordings from 86 participants from the Brain, Body, and Behavior Dataset. Using hidden Markov modelling, we identified recurrent multimodal states after accounting for stable recording-level differences and stimulus-shared responses. Three reproducible states with distinct psychophysiological profiles emerged. Poorer subsequent quiz performance was associated with greater relative expression of a state characterized by longer fixations, reduced fixation and saccade rates, lower gaze entropy, elevated pupil level and variability, and distinct EEG spectral entropy and frontoparietal theta coherence. In contrast, better performance was associated with greater expression of a state characterized primarily by more frequent and larger phasic pupil dilations. Quiz performance was also positively associated with transitions from this phasic-pupil state to the dominant background state, whereas relative expression of the dominant state itself showed no robust association with performance. The transition association did not survive correction in common-record window-length sensitivity analyses. These findings indicate that learning during naturalistic viewing is associated with the dynamic coordination of multiple ocular, pupillary, and neural signals, with relative state balance and directed transition probabilities each associated with subsequent quiz performance.

papers.title: Distinct experience-dependent reorganization of rhythmic syllable tracking in 6-month-old term and preterm infants
papers.abstract: Preterm birth increases the risk of later language difficulties, yet its impact on early neural mechanisms supporting language acquisition, including speech rhythm tracking, remains understudied. Using EEG, we measured neural tracking of delta- and theta-rate syllable sequences produced by the infant's mother or an unfamiliar speaker in term and preterm 6-month-old infants, modeling how oscillatory responses evolved over the course of a testing session. Term infants progressively strengthened frequency-matched delta tuning over all frontotemporal regions, whereas preterm infants did so only over the right temporal region. Over left frontal channels, this divergence was one of frequency selectivity: term infants became increasingly selective for the delta rhythm, whereas preterm infants showed no reliable selectivity. The frontal group difference emerged only with the unfamiliar speaker, where term infants' build-up of delta tuning was largely specific. Preterm birth is thus associated with a different refinement of frequency-specific tuning during exposure, rather than with a general weakness in tracking speech rhythm, identifying a candidate neural pathway with implications for early language learning.

papers.title: Pre-anaesthetic anxiety phenotype stratifies anaesthesia EEG, acquired navigation, and post-anaesthesia sleep in sevoflurane-exposed mice
papers.abstract: Preoperative anxiety is common and has been associated with postoperative delirium, yet whether an anxious phenotype changes the brain's response to anaesthesia is unknown. Here, 42 mice are classified as low-anxiety (LA) or high-anxiety (HA) by fear-retrieval freezing and exposed to sevoflurane without surgery. When adequate anaesthetic effects are reached, HA mice show a higher aperiodic spectral edge frequency than LA mice. After anaesthesia, both groups retain choice accuracy in the Water Cross Maze, but in the same trials decomposed into behavioural syllables, the learned navigation sequence is selectively disrupted in HA mice. Rapid eye-movement sleep decreases in HA mice and increases in LA mice. A single anxiety phenotype defined before induction therefore tracks three responses to the same sevoflurane exposure. These findings suggest that pre-anaesthetic anxiety marks individual vulnerability to anaesthesia in mice. The results may pave the way to interventions preserving cognitive function and sleep during perioperative recovery.

papers.title: Enhanced KNa1.1 Channel Underlies Cortical Hyperexcitability and Seizure Susceptibility after Traumatic Brain Injury
papers.abstract: Pathogenic variants of the sodium-activated potassium channel KNa1.1 have been reported in multiple epileptic disorders. However, whether and how KNa1.1 channel is involved in epileptogenesis after traumatic brain injury (TBI) remains unknown. Firstly, we used behavioral monitoring and EEG recording to examine physiological property, spontaneous seizure activity, and seizure susceptibility after TBI. We explored the changes of KNa1.1 channel following TBI, including changes of subcellular distribution and expression pattern. Meanwhile, we performed patch-clamp recording to detect the neuronal excitability. Furthermore, we built TBI model using kcnt1-/- mice and compared seizure susceptibility and electrophysiological properties with those of wild-type mice. We found severity-dependent seizure susceptibility in different degree of injured mice. Meanwhile, increased neuronal expression of KNa1.1 channel around the lesion was also observed following TBI, accompanied by a reduced firing rate of interneurons and imbalanced excitation and inhibition (E/I). Although the maximum frequency of action potential of kcnt1-/- neurons was increased, kcnt1-/- mice displayed decreased seizure susceptibility to the pentylenetetrazole (PTZ) after TBI. In kcnt1-/- mice, TBI did not significantly alter afterhyperpolarization amplitude or action-potential firing frequency in pyramidal neurons or interneurons; although the frequencies of both sEPSCs and sIPSCs increased, the E/I ratio remained unchanged. Taken together, this study suggests that enhancedKNa1.1 expression after TBI contributes to disputed E/I balance and seizure susceptibility, and that KNa1.1 might be a potential therapeutic target for reducing seizure susceptibility after TBI.

papers.title: Dynamic hippocampal and cortical signatures of naturalistic event memory
papers.abstract: Remembering temporally extended experiences requires integrating information over time into coherent event representations that can be stored and later retrieved. This process places changing demands on memory as an event unfolds: event representations must be reset at the beginning, connected into a unified model during the event, and stored in long-term memory at the end. We hypothesized that oscillatory dynamics, by coordinating communication across regions and organizing neural activity in time, provide a flexible mechanism for meeting these changing demands. However, most evidence comes from discrete-stimulus paradigms, leaving unclear how they support continuous experience. We recorded intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG) while participants watched a movie and later freely recalled it, and tested how power, phase synchrony and alignment at the beginning, middle, and end of each event related to subsequent memory. At beginnings, remembered events showed reduced gamma power and increased hippocampal-frontal synchrony. Within an event, memory was predicted by increasing temporal gamma power and hippocampal-temporal gamma synchrony, consistent with progressive binding of information. At event endings, memory was reflected by increased hippocampal theta power and phase resetting. Together these results provide a new perspective on how the brain supports memory in naturalistic settings, showing that it does not rest on one sustained encoding state. Instead, it requires temporal coordination of oscillatory states across brain regions and event phases, in which stable states support ongoing representation while transient, boundary-driven reorganization of hippocampal-cortical networks switches the system between storing the completed event and encoding the next. Significance StatementTheories about how brain rhythms support memory have assumed a single optimal brain state for encoding new information, based on studies presenting discrete items, such as words or images. Real-world experience, however, is continuous: events unfold over time and are encoded as connected memory traces. By recording electrical brain activity while patients watched and recalled a 50-minute film, we find that remembering an event depends not on one static encoding state but on a dynamic sequence of brain rhythms and hippocampal-cortical coordination that change as the event begins, unfolds, and ends. These findings show that previous discrete-item paradigms capture only a snapshot of one step in memory formation and reveal how the brain converts continuous experience into lasting memories.

papers.title: An expanded GRAB sensor palette for multiplexed imaging of purinergic dynamics in vivo
papers.abstract: Extracellular ATP and adenosine operate as tightly coupled purinergic signals, yet tracking both molecules simultaneously in vivo has been limited by the performance and spectral range of existing sensors. We describe an expanded set of genetically encoded GPCR-Activation-Based (GRAB) sensors for ATP and adenosine that together support multiplexed imaging of purinergic signaling in the intact brain. Systematic optimization of receptor scaffolds, membrane trafficking, and fluorophore coupling yielded next-generation green sensors (Ado2h, Ado2m, ATP2h, ATP2l) and spectrally separated red variants (rAdo1h, rATP1h), each combining high ligand specificity, genetically targetable expression, sub-second kinetics, and minimal engagement of endogenous GPCR pathways. This combination allows minimally invasive, dual-color imaging of purinergic activity in vivo. Using multiplexed fiber photometry and two-photon imaging, we tracked ATP and adenosine concurrently across several behavioral and pathological settings. ATP release preceded extracellular adenosine accumulation during sleep-wake transitions and neuronal activation, a pattern consistent with extracellular ATP hydrolysis as a substantial contributor to in vivo adenosine signaling. During epileptic seizures, paired imaging of extracellular ATP with extracellular adenosine, and of extracellular with intracellular adenosine, indicated distinct spatiotemporal dynamics across cellular compartments. This expanded sensor set offers a platform for multiplexed purinergic imaging and for probing ATP-adenosine coupling across physiological and pathological brain states.

papers.title: Behaviorally driven increased glutamatergic activity from lateral entorhinal cortex to hippocampus supports object and spatial memory recall
papers.abstract: Interactions between the entorhinal cortex (EC) and hippocampal area CA1 are vital for episodic memory formation, but their role in recall is less clear. Canonically, spatial processing -- the "where" of an experience -- is attributed to the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC), whereas the lateral entorhinal cortex (LEC) processes the "what": non-spatial sensory cues and objects. Though these inputs are anatomically segregated in CA1, multimodal memory processing requires integrating spatial and contextual information, and recent work suggests greater MEC-LEC crosstalk than previously thought. Global LEC silencing via lesions, or combined suppression of glutamatergic and GABAergic LEC neurons, impairs associational goal-oriented learning and multi-object-cued encoding. However, the role of LEC glutamatergic projections specifically to CA1 during recall in freely moving spatial behaviors, and their contribution to synaptic plasticity, remains unclear. We used fiber photometry to record LEC axonal calcium dynamics in CA1 during novel object recognition and Barnes maze tasks, and ex vivo electrophysiology with LEC optogenetic activation. LEC activity increased during recall in both tasks, especially as animals learned spatial cues, peaking at late training stages of the Barnes maze. Local chemogenetic silencing of LEC inputs in CA1 after learning impaired recall. Ex vivo, temporally precise optogenetic activation of LEC input paired with CA3 intrahippocampal inputs was sufficient to induce long-term potentiation of both pathways in CA1 pyramidal neurons. These results suggest that LEC glutamatergic input to CA1 is dynamically modulated by experience to support recall during both object recognition and spatial navigation, with a functional role in synaptic plasticity.

papers.title: One More Night: Investigating the Stability of Verbal Overnight Memory Consolidation and Sources of Variability
papers.abstract: Sleep-Dependent Memory Consolidation (SDMC) plays a vital role in facilitating the retention of newly learnt information. However, retesting in the literature is scarce and thus little is known regarding the daily stability of the SDMC process. The present study investigated whether overnight memory consolidation performance is stable (reflecting a trait) or variable (reflecting a state) across two nights using a novel word-pair smartphone application. Furthermore, the study examined the influence of subjective sleep quality and motivation on overnight consolidation performance, and whether these associations remained consistent across nights. Young healthy adults (N = 52) completed a validated word-pair task via a smartphone application over two nights and completed subjective sleep and motivation questionnaires. Results indicated overnight consolidation performance was not stable across nights, despite same-day and next-day recall exhibiting significant stability. Subjective sleep and motivation scores were not associated with performance, although these associations remained consistent across nights. However, worse PSQI scores were associated with lower next-day recall. After considering semantically related and unrelated word-pairs, both same-day and next-day recall performance exhibited significant stability for unrelated word-pairs only. These findings question the reliance on single-night SDMC protocols, and future research should examine modifiable factors that underlie SDMC variability across nights.

papers.title: Forecasting Human Sleep Dynamics with a Latent-State Framework
papers.abstract: Sleep is essential for health, and forecasting its evolution could clarify its temporal organization and guide intervention timing. We developed a representation-forecasting model using electroencephalography from 5,419 participants. From 30-minute histories, 10-minute forecasts achieved 90.71% four-class accuracy in the 10% of windows with lowest predicted risk and averaged 72.11% overall. Direction-specific encoder feature axes had spectral correlates. Forecast changes under fixed-strength perturbations along these axes can quantify window-specific sensitivity varying with observed transition destination and bout timing. Physiological validation linked greater simulated perturbation sensitivity to stronger observed sleep-state responses following acoustic stimulation and respiratory events. Clinical profiling linked older age and higher apnoea-hypopnoea index to stronger modeled Wake-directed and weaker N3-directed responses. These results demonstrated that sleep-state forecasting could quantify dynamics, prioritize candidate intervention windows, and help interpret post-intervention changes.

papers.title: Local sleep in wake is widespread across the rat cortex and tracks sleep need
papers.abstract: During non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, cortical neurons alternate between ON periods of firing and OFF periods of silence, the latter accounting for the slow waves of the EEG. Converging evidence indicates that OFF periods can also occur locally during extended wake ("local sleep"), at a behavioral cost, but whether this phenomenon is ubiquitous across the cortex, whether some areas are more resilient than others, and whether it can also provide any benefit, remain open questions. Here we recorded from 11 cortical areas (and claustrum) in 15 rats using high-density Neuropixels probes and detected OFF periods with a novel method that captures spatially restricted and irregularly shaped events mischaracterized or missed by traditional methods. We found OFF periods during extended wake in every region tested, with no evidence that any area is spared. Over the course of sleep deprivation, OFF periods became more frequent, longer, larger, and quieter, and their features correlated with delta power on a per-event basis in both wake and NREM sleep, consistent with the notion that they reflect accumulating sleep need. The extent to which OFF periods overlapped across areas also increased across sleep deprivation. Finally, the rate of medium and large OFF periods during sleep deprivation was negatively correlated with their rebound in subsequent recovery sleep, consistent with the possibility that local sleep in wake partially discharges sleep need before the animal falls asleep. Statement of SignificanceProlonged wakefulness drives small groups of cortical neurons into brief sleep-like states even as the animal remains awake and behaving. This "local sleep" in wake is thought to underlie the errors and slowed responses of sleep deprivation, but how widespread it is, and whether it helps, remains unclear. Using high-density recordings across many cortical regions in the rat and a novel detection method sensitive to small, irregular events, we show that local sleep is not confined to a few vulnerable areas but occurs throughout the cortex, growing with accumulating sleep need. We also find that these neuronal lapses may begin to relieve that need before sleep takes over, suggesting that they may represent an early, piecemeal form of recovery.

papers.title: Evidence supporting resting-state power spectrum exponent as a non-invasive measure of neural-circuit excitation:inhibition balance in children with and without autism
papers.abstract: IntroductionAn ongoing neural circuit excitation (E) and inhibition (I) imbalance is thought to be a major contributor to clinical conditions such as autism, schizophrenia, and epilepsy. Current methods for directly measuring E:I dynamics require invasive procedures that are difficult to perform in non-human animals and nearly impossible in humans. A non-invasive measure of E:I balance is of great interest as a diagnostic as well as therapeutic marker, and as a means of studying relevant pathological and intervention mechanisms. Scientists have recently developed a computational model to show that, using resting-state (RS) MEG or EEG recordings, the E:I balance can be estimated from the power law exponent (slope) of the electrophysiological power spectrum. In their model, the RS power spectrum exponent is hypothesized to reflect the integration of synaptic currents in the brain, an index of E:I balance driven largely by excitatory (glutamate, Glu) and inhibitory (gamma-aminobutyric acid, GABA) neurotransmitter levels. Glu and GABA are the principal excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitters in the brain, together shaping the balance between neural circuit excitation and inhibition. The present study shows that parietal-occipital neurochemistry as a predictor of the parietal-occipital RS exponent is driven by inhibitory neurotransmitter levels in typically developing (TD) children but not in children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). MethodsMidline parietal-occipital RS power spectra (MEG) and Glu and GABA+ concentration (MRS) were obtained from 129 children (TD N = 84, ASD N = 45) 10.2 to 17.9 years old, with follow-up measures in a subset of the children providing 148 MEG and MRS datasets. Analyses focused on RS neural function and Glu and GABA+ concentration in parietal-occipital cortex. Resultst-tests showed no group differences between the parietal-occipital exponent, Glu, GABA+, or Glu/GABA+ ratio measures (ps > 0.21). In the full sample, older age was marginally associated with a lower exponent (p = 0.07), and older age associated with lower Glu concentration (p < 0.05). Age and GABA concentration or Glu/GABA+ associations were not observed (p > 0.05). There was no main effect of Glu or Glu x Group interaction with the exponent (ps > 0.14). Simple effect analyses of group interactions for GABA+ (p < 0.05) and ratio (p<0.05) showed a GABA+ and exponent association for TD (p = 0.01) but not ASD (p = 0.40) and a ratio and exponent association for TD (p = 0.01) but not ASD (p = 0.83). DiscussionThe brain chemistry and RS exponent associations suggest that a simple method for estimating E:I ratio reduces a major hurdle in understanding a currently difficult-to-measure, yet fundamental aspect of neural computation that has been proposed as central to clinical conditions such as ASD, epilepsy, and schizophrenia. Present findings indicate that the contribution of local brain chemistry to neural-circuit E:I balance differs for older children with and without ASD, with GABA inhibition presenting the more promising contributor to the E:I balance in TD children. Findings have the potential for high impact, including identifying neural markers for use in tracking treatment response.

papers.title: Top-down prefrontal connectivity accompanies perceptual breakthrough after interocular suppression
papers.abstract: The role of the prefrontal cortex (PFC) in the emergence of visual stimuli into conscious awareness remains contested. Additionally, whether top-down prefrontal connectivity is shaped by prior expectations during this process is not well understood. To address these questions, we applied dynamic causal modelling (DCM) to an EEG dataset during breaking continuous flash suppression (bCFS), which offers tight control over when a stimulus breaks into conscious perception. Our network comprised bilateral PFC, primary visual cortex, fusiform gyrus and motor cortex. Because perceptual breakthrough precedes behavioural report, we used a temporally resolved classifier to empirically define each participants moment of perceptual breakthrough (M = 1250ms, SD = 100ms). DCMs were then inverted over this time window up until each individuals breakthrough point. Parametric empirical Bayes revealed that top-down connectivity from the PFC to all regions was necessary to explain the observed neural dynamics (posterior probability [pp] > 0.99), though evidence that this top-down influence was modulated by expectation was inconclusive (pp = 0.74). Together, these findings suggest that top-down PFC connectivity accompanies perceptual breakthrough in bCFS, but it remains unclear whether this is modulated by expectation.

papers.title: Predictive coding networks capture human neural representations missing in supervised DNNs
papers.abstract: Neuroscientific learning theories propose that the brain acquires knowledge by constructing internal world models. Supervised learning, the dominant approach in deep neural networks (DNN), relies on external category labels, making it difficult to reconcile with biological learning. There is an increasing trend towards more biologically valid approaches, such as predictive (minimize future surprise) or contrastive (minimize response to expected, maximize to unexpected inputs) objectives, but these approaches typically rely on pretrained DNN models that vary widely in architecture, size, and hyperparameters, making direct comparisons difficult. Here, we isolate the effect of learning by comparing small, identical networks trained with predictive, contrastive, and supervised learning objectives, as well as local (layer-restricted) vs. global (full backpropagation) learning. Using representational similarity analysis of a previously acquired EEG dataset, we show that brain representations after statistical learning are better modeled by a predictive local learning than supervised or contrastive learning, and that during learning, the brain attenuates category-specific representations while retaining predictive ones. We additionally show that predictive objectives explain brain variance that standard supervised DNNs do not, and that this variance is tied to predictive rather than stimulus or mismatch processing. These findings demonstrate a controlled approach for testing the algorithmic basis of learning and identify prediction as a core learning mechanism.

papers.title: Mechanistic insights into state-dependent synchronization of neural activity by weak tACS fields
papers.abstract: Transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) biases spike timing with weak electric fields, but how re- current circuitry and network state shape this response is unclear. We simulated tACS in a detailed cortical column model in two network states of varying coherence, roughly corresponding to REM-like and NREM-like states. Despite weak impacts on network firing rates, stimulation entrained network activity at realistically occurring field strengths. Global entrainment was initiated by direct entrainment of ongoing pyramidal cell activity, which subsequently recruited inhibitory interneurons in a state-dependent manner. The NREM-like network locked more strongly to all tested stimulation frequencies, independent of baseline spectral power, and displayed larger recurrent-connectivity-mediated phase lags. However, recurrent connectivity was not required for, and did not amplify, entrainment, but instead produced an offset in baseline network activity. Our re- sults highlight the impact of network state on the response to tACS, and suggest that meso-scale models of electromagnetic-electrophysiological interactions must look beyond single-cell polarization and baseline oscilla- tions at the stimulation frequency.

papers.title: Relative distance change rather than absolute distance drives auditory alerting
papers.abstract: The function of hearing as an early warning system relies partly on detecting the distance and motion of an object based on sound. Approaching - or looming - objects activate the human alerting system, but it is debated whether sounds in the immediate vicinity of the body achieve the same irrespective of the direction of motion and of sound intensity. We addressed this question by examining distance perception of and phasic alertness states evoked by virtual sonic motion into and within peripersonal and extrapersonal space, at high and low intensities, in normal-hearing adults. Based on distance ratings, target detection promptness, and electroencephalography (EEG), we found that looming auditory objects increase phasic alertness and auditory sensory gain, and we also observed a general tendency to perceive sound offsets as closer to the body than onsets. However, we did not find evidence that auditory objects moving at a constant distance within peripersonal space affect alerting over and above the influence of intensity. We suggest that the auditory looming bias is not amplified further by preferential processing of auditory information near the body, and that the early warning function of hearing emphasizes the direction of motion over distance.

papers.title: DualBranchEEG: A Dual-Branch CNN BiLSTM Network with Temporal Attention and Spectral Features for Three Class EEG Seizure Classification
papers.abstract: Automated seizure detection from electroencephalography (EEG) is a key step toward closed-loop brain-computer interface (BCI) systems and clinical decision support. We present DualBranchEEG, a dual-branch network that fuses (i) a temporal branch--a three-block 1-D convolutional encoder, a two-layer bidirectional LSTM and an additive attention layer--operating on the raw z-scored waveform, with (ii) a spectral branch--an MLP on log-power spectral density (PSD) features from Welch's method. We evaluate three-class classification (normal, interictal, ictal) on the Bonn University EEG dataset (500 single-channel recordings, 173.61 Hz) using a single stratified 70/15/15 split (seed 42). We position this work as a transparent reference implementation and exploratory comparison, not as evidence of superiority. A CNN-BiLSTM baseline (728,387 parameters; last-time-step readout, no attention, no augmentation) attains 96.00% test accuracy (72/75) and a macro AUC-ROC of 0.9795; five-fold stratified cross-validation of this baseline gives 98.40 {+/-} 1.52% accuracy and 0.9952 {+/-} 0.0071 AUC-ROC. The full DualBranchEEG (823,556 parameters) attains the same 96.00% test accuracy, macro F1 of 0.9543 and macro AUC-ROC of 0.9952. In the ablation, CNN-only, BiLSTM-only and CNN+BiLSTM+attention variants each reach 94.67%, and the full model is one test recording better; with only 75 test recordings these differences lie within sampling uncertainty (95% Wilson interval for 96.00%: 88.9-98.6%). Band-power differences between all class pairs are significant in all five canonical EEG bands. Grad-CAM, t-SNE and attention visualisations are reported as qualitative diagnostics only. We document all known methodological limitations, including PSD standardisation fitted on all 500 recordings and Welch's default 50% segment overlap.

papers.title: Causal dissociation of occipital and mid-fusiform contributions to human visual experience
papers.abstract: Visual experiences can arise without corresponding retinal input, as in imagery, dreams, and hallucinations. Influential models of visual mental imagery propose that mental images acquire their visual quality in early visual cortex. Direct intracranial electrical cortical stimulation (DIECS) causally probes which cortical sites can evoke visual experiences, and of what kind. We examined de novo visual experiences evoked by stimulation in three patients undergoing stereo-EEG monitoring for drug-resistant epilepsy and localized the effective contact pairs using the Julich-Brain cytoarchitectonic atlas. Among the sampled sites, stimulation of occipital and adjacent intraparietal cortex and of the posterior fusiform area FG1 elicited simple or intermediate phenomena, including flashes, colored spots, and elementary shapes. By contrast, only stimulation of sites in or adjacent to the mid-fusiform areas FG3 and FG4 elicited complex images of people, scenes, and objects. These findings provide cytoarchitectonically localized causal evidence that stimulation of right mid-fusiform cortex can trigger complex visual experiences, possibly through distributed networks. They also identify the mid-fusiform gyrus as a promising causal node for complex visual content, and are compatible with lesion and neuroimaging evidence challenging the necessity of early visual cortex for visual imagery.

papers.title: Brain rhythms during Instagram Reels viewing and subsequent performance on sustained attention and working memory: an EEG study
papers.abstract: What does even a short scrolling 'snack' do to the brain? Short-form video feeds such as Instagram Reels have been rapidly becoming a near-universal phenomenon, used widely by people around the world, especially young adults. However, this is a very recent development, and yet their immediate effects on brain activity, attention, and working memory remain unclear. In a counterbalanced, within-subject experiment, we examined whether 10 minutes of Instagram Reels altered electroencephalographic (EEG) activity, cognitive performance, and subjective fatigue. Thirty university students completed three testing blocks separated by two counterbalanced interventions selected from viewing Reels on their own accounts, viewing a silent sequence of neutral images on their phones, or resting with eyes closed. EEG was recorded using 65 electrodes during interventions and subsequent sustained-attention (SART) and working-memory (N-back) tasks. Compared with neutral images, Reels viewing was associated with higher posterior relative theta power and a lower posterior alpha-to-theta ratio. During the subsequent N-back, frontal relative alpha was higher after Reels than after neutral images. Fatigue increased more after Reels than after rest. One of four planned contrasts in the cleaned sample was significant. Brief Reels viewing was associated with differences in EEG activity compared with viewing neutral images, while no significant differences in attention or working-memory performance were detected after correction for multiple comparisons.

papers.title: Acute Effects of Prolonged Intermittent Theta Burst Stimulation on Cortical Excitability: A Randomized Crossover TMS-EEG Study
papers.abstract: Background: prolonged intermittent theta burst stimulation (piTBS), as used in Stanford Neuromodulation Therapy (SNT), achieves antidepressant efficacy, yet its acute single-session mechanisms remain elusive. EEG can capture online oscillatory dynamics during piTBS and pre- to post-stimulation changes in TMS-evoked cortical reactivity. Methods: in a randomized, sham-controlled crossover trial, 40 healthy males completed two visits ( [≥]7-day washout), receiving active or sham piTBS over the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. Inter-train EEG power was analyzed across three blocks of 20 trains in 37 participants. Pre- and post-stimulation measures of TMS-evoked potentials (TEPs), working memory and sustained attention were analyzed in all 40 participants. Results: left frontal theta power followed different trajectories across blocks during active and sham piTBS (conditionxblock interaction, p = .014). During active piTBS, theta power was below baseline in blocks 1 and 2 and increased significantly from block 2 to block 3. Across conditions, alpha power was lower in blocks 2 and 3 than in block 1. Direct comparison of pre-to-post TEP changes between active and sham piTBS identified no significant clusters in the N45, P60, N100 and P180 component windows. Exploratory analyses within active piTBS identified a decrease in frontal N100 cluster amplitude and an increase in posterior N100 cluster amplitude. Neither behavioral outcome showed condition-dependent changes. Conclusion: a single session of active piTBS modulated left frontal theta power between stimulation trains. Whether this early response is associated with cumulative plasticity or antidepressant outcomes following SNT warrants further investigation.

papers.title: Focused Ultrasound Neuromodulation: Disentangling Neural Signals from Mechanical Artifacts
papers.abstract: Transcranial focused ultrasound (tFUS) can noninvasively modulate neural activity in the human brain (Blackmore et al., 2019; Fomenko et al., 2018; Legon et al., 2014), and EEG, with millisecond resolution, is well suited to track the timing of cortical engagement. In humans, tFUS aimed at primary visual cortex (V1) has been reported to evoke phosphenes, with EEG peaks (N55, P100) during sonication (Lee et al., 2016). Ultrasound can also activate cortex indirectly through the auditory pathway (Sato et al., 2018), although airborne sound from the transducer can be masked (Braun et al., 2020; Liang et al., 2023). Whether the N55 and P100 peaks reflect neuronal activation or artifacts (i.e., non-neuronal signals produced by the ultrasound itself) is unclear. We set out to ask whether EEG decoding could detect neural engagement during tFUS to V1 in eight participants receiving 150 or 300-ms pulses or sham. Decoding of tFUS versus sham reached as much as 93% for exactly the duration of each pulse (cluster p = .004 and .008), with no later cluster significant. But the same pulse-locked step appeared on all channels, scaled with drive, and was also recorded from a foam head and a forehead piezo pickup, identifying it as mechanical. Decoding during sonication must therefore be interpreted as a mechanical artifact rather than cortical engagement. EEG peaks observed within a pulse cannot on their own be taken as evidence of neural engagement. EEG studies of tFUS will need controls that reproduce the vibration without focusing on the brain, such as an active sham.
